claims.text: A nanoscale silver coating can be deposited on tungsten particles before W–Cu composite consolidation.
The intervention produces a nanoscale silver layer at the interface between tungsten particles and the copper matrix.
The interfacial silver layer reduces phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
The interfacial silver layer reduces electron scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Reduced phonon and electron scattering lowers the thermal boundary resistance of the W–Cu interface.
Silver can form robust interfacial bonds in the proposed W–Cu composite.
High silver conductivity and robust interfacial bonding help preserve the composite's mechanical strength.
High silver conductivity and robust interfacial bonding help preserve the composite's performance under irradiation.
Silver-coated W–Cu composites will have higher effective thermal conductivity than otherwise comparable composites containing uncoated tungsten particles.
Silver-coated W–Cu composites will retain mechanical durability comparable to the uncoated baseline.
Silver-coated W–Cu composites will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The proposed benefit is expected under the high thermal loads and neutron irradiation associated with heat-dissipation components and fusion-reactor joints.
The benefit depends on optimizing the thickness and chemical stability of the silver coating.
An excessively thick, reactive, or microstructure-disrupting silver coating could diminish the anticipated benefits.
Extreme irradiation or thermal cycling could diminish the coating's benefits.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement is uncertain without optimization.
The long-term irradiation stability of the silver interface has not been established.
